sentences.text: Torvosaurus tanneri measured around 9 meters long and weighed approximately 2 to 2.4 metric tons, while specimens of T. gurneyi reached up to 10 meters in length and 4 to 5 metric tons.
The holotype and paratypes of Torvosaurus represented at least three individuals: two adults and one juvenile.
The specific name tanneri honors Nathan Eldon Tanner, a first counselor in the First Presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
The first remains referable to Torvosaurus were discovered in 1899 by Elmer Riggs in the Freeze-out Hills of southeastern Wyoming.
The genus Torvosaurus was named by Peter Malcolm Galton and James Alvin Jensen in 1979.
Remains of a large theropod now believed to be Torvosaurus were discovered in the Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania and named Megalosaurus ingens by Werner Janensch in 1920.
Teeth of a member of the genus Torvosaurus were described from the Tacuarembó Formation of Uruguay by Soto et al. in 2020.
The highly porous eggshells of Torvosaurus indicate the eggs were buried in the substrate for incubation, similar to modern sea turtles.
All documented Torvosaurus specimens from the Morrison Formation appear to be similarly sized, likely adult individuals.
Torvosaurus appears to have been the top predator in the Lourinhã Formation ecosystem.
When first described in 1979 by Galton and Jensen, Torvosaurus was classified as a megalosaurid, which remains the current consensus.
Torvosaurus was later assigned to Carnosauria in 1990, to a basal position in Spinosauroidea in 2003, and to a very basal position in Tetanurae in 1994.
In 1985, Jensen assigned Torvosaurus to its own family, Torvosauridae.
Most researchers now regard Edmarka rex and Brontoraptor as junior synonyms of Torvosaurus tanneri.
Torvosaurus lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic periods, specifically from the Callovian to the Tithonian ages.
Torvosaurus contains two recognized species, T. tanneri and T. gurneyi, and one unnamed species from Germany.
Fossils of Torvosaurus have been found in what is now Colorado, Portugal, Germany, and possibly England, Spain, Tanzania, and Uruguay.
This indicates derived megalosaurines were among the largest terrestrial predators in the late Middle Jurassic, with only moderate size increases by the Late Jurassic.
It is debated whether teeth from Tanzania and Uruguay belong to Torvosaurus, as some researchers consider them undiagnostic and similar to other theropods like carcharodontosaurids.

Researchers debate whether Megalosaurus ingens from Tanzania and Uruguayan teeth represent the same taxon as Torvosaurus, noting shared features but lacking derived characteristics to confirm synonymy.
It is debated whether Edmarka rex and Brontoraptor are junior synonyms of Torvosaurus tanneri, as their original specimens lack detailed descriptions for confirmation.
In 2012, Matthew Carrano and colleagues concluded that Portuguese fossils could not be identified more precisely than Torvosaurus sp.
